newsitem.title: JAPAN: BOJ policy inertia to flatten yield curve - traders.
newsitem.headline: BOJ policy inertia to flatten yield curve - traders.

text.p: The Bank of Japan's inertia on monetary policy is likely to flatten out the yield curve of the Japanese government bond (JGB) market, senior economists and money traders said on Thursday.

The BOJ's quarterly "tankan" corporate survey, a vital clue to the central bank's policy, on Wednesday reinforced the market conviction that a credit tightening, if any, will not come before mid-1997, they said.
Against this background, the key 10-year JGB yield dived to a record low of 2.390 percent on Thursday.

"Chances are that the central bank will be able to remove the current cap on short-term rates and let them firm a little in summer 1997," said Shoji Kitta, managing director of Tokyo Tanchi Co Ltd, the largest money broker in Japan.
The BOJ capped the key overnight call rate in September 1995 at 0.5 percent, the level of the official discount rate (ODR), and has kept it there since then.

"However, their option of raising the ODR will be left unexercised unless the key diffusion index (DI) for major manufacturers shows nearly double-digit growth, which may be seen in the tankan a year from now," Kitta said.

In Wednesday's tankan survey, the widely watched forecast for the diffusion index of major manufacturers' business sentiment next March stayed in negative territory at minus one, only a slight improvement in mood.

"The yield curve will flatten further, with the benchmark 10-year JGB yield heading towards two percent," said Shin Nagai, money market manager of the Treasury Department at ABN AMRO Bank's Tokyo branch.
But the BOJ is unlikely to allow a further rate drop in the short end of the curve, in view of the government's economic assessment, which is more optimistic than the market, he added.

"It is too early to conclude that the tax rise will substantially reduce consumption in 1997/98," Masayuki Matsushima, the director of the BOJ's research and statistics department, said on Wednesday. He was referring to a controversial rise in Japan's consumption tax due in April.
Yet a variety of bullish factors are backing the JGB rally.

Taisuke Tanaka, market strategist at Credit Suisse's Tokyo branch, said: "The JGBs are gaining strength from a combination of bullish factors such as a non-expansionary budget policy for the next year along with a tax hike and a discontinuation of special income tax cuts, on top of weak corporate sentiment and institutional investor demand."

The yield spread between three-month and 10-year JGBs will narrow further, with a chance of a temporary widening ahead of the corporate annual book closings at the end of March, Tanaka said. This is because high-performing JGBs could become a target for profit-taking for window-dressing purposes.

Meanwhile, the short-end yield is unlikely to come down further, not only because of the relatively optimistic economic view held by the government, but because more liquidity injection by the BOJ would do little to rejuvenate the real economy, Tanaka said. Key three-month certificates of deposit were traded at 0.50 percent on Thursday.
Liquidity supplied by the central bank has been flowing more into savings and the financial markets than into capital investment due to companies' bearish mood on the economy, Tanaka said.
The JGBs are also being helped by the government's slowness in crafting measures to raise liquidity in the land market, the lack of which lies at the core of Japan's bad loan problems, Kitta said.
Economists said that more financial woes at regional banks are likely to surface in December, underscoring the need for the BOJ to maintain its ultra-easy credit grip.
